title: Greed, the never-enough thief

cards: One more pair of shoes. One more thing in the cart. One more raise, and then life can relax.

Greed rarely calls itself greed. It calls itself almost there. The finish line keeps sliding forward, and the runner pays for it in sleep, in worry, in evenings not spent with the people in the next room.
Guru Nanak put his finger on this in the very first pauri of the Japji, the hymn Sikhs recite in the morning. Today's thief is lobh, the one that never says enough.

teach.b: First, the hunger. In the opening pauri of the Japji, in paraphrase: the hunger of the hungry does not go away, even if they pile up loads of the world's goods. Bhukhiaa bhukh na utree.
It isn't a threat; it's an observation. The pile grows, and the hunger stays exactly where it was. Second, an image that sticks.
In a hymn in Sri Rag, Guru Nanak lines up the vices as low company.

In paraphrase: greed is a dog, falsehood is the sweeper, and cheating is eating carrion. Greed as a dog: nose down, always sniffing for the next scrap, never full, never off duty. Third, a story Sikhs tell.
The janamsakhis, the old stories of Guru Nanak's life, say that in Saidpur he stayed with Bhai Lalo, a carpenter who earned his bread with his own hands.
A rich official, Malik Bhago, held a grand feast and expected the Guru, who didn't come.
Pressed for a reason, the story goes, he took Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and Bhago's fine food in the other, and squeezed. From Lalo's bread came milk. From Bhago's, blood.
Wealth wrung out of other people carries what it cost them.
Fourth, the cure isn't poverty. Sikhs are taught to work hard, earn honestly and share. Lobh isn't having money.
It's never letting any of it be enough, and never letting any of it go. The word that stops this thief is very small. Enough.

how: Sikhs count lobh, greed, among the five thieves; the Sikh answer is honest work (kirat), sharing (vand chhakna) and contentment, not renouncing money, and the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago is often told to make the point.

o: wanting good things for the people you love
saving money carefully for the future
the hunger that never lets anything be enough

games.q: the never-enough thief: tap the pairs.
p: the hunger doesn't go, says the Japji

s: Sikh teaching says having money is greed
Sikhs are taught to earn honestly and share. lobh is never letting it be enough.
the Japji says piling up goods won't end the hunger
bhukhiaa bhukh na utree: the hunger of the hungry doesn't go away.
Guru Nanak compares greed to a dog
in Sri Rag: greed a dog, falsehood the sweeper.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak in Saidpur. a rich official has laid out a grand feast and expects you. a carpenter has coarse bread he earned by hand. where do you eat?
o: at the feast; refusing would be rude.
with the carpenter, on his coarse bread.
games.why: the story says he stayed with Bhai Lalo, and when pressed, squeezed both: milk from Lalo's bread, blood from Bhago's.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you keep reaching for more of, money, likes, food, praise, hours at work, and just see it, without scolding yourself. On each breath out, let the single word enough be the whole sentence.
Between breaths, notice what's already in your hands, a roof, a meal, a person, this breath, and if you pray, give thanks for one of them.

wordCard.voice: Greed. Lobh: the thief that never lets anything be enough, the dog that's never full. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: greed, the appetite that keeps moving the finish line; in the Granth often ਲੋਭੁ.

carryVoice: Your line: enough. One small word against a hunger that never fills. Same time tomorrow.
